metadata.title: The Polling Problem
metadata.purpose: STEM & AI Architecture, Week 9 — event-driven architecture: why polling wastes compute on slow AI work, what a webhook actually is, how one POST fans out through an orchestrator, and the delivery guarantee you give up to get decoupling.

beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Onkar Bhujbal. If you have two systems that need to talk to each other, the worst thing you can do is have one constantly ask the other for updates. That is polling, and it wastes enormous amounts of compute. Today we are looking at event-driven architecture, and why A.I. applications rely on the don't-call-us-we'll-call-you approach known as webhooks.

props.command: My app asks the model service "are you done yet?" every two seconds. Why am I hitting rate limits?

beats.honesty_note: The 40s / 2s / 20 requests figures are ARITHMETIC from the script's own framing (it cites AI jobs taking 30 seconds to several minutes), not a measurement of any system. 19 of 20 returning empty follows directly.

beats.narration_text: Polling asks a question over and over until the answer changes. An event tells you once, when it changes. Everything else in this video is a consequence of that one swap.

props.text:
Ask repeatedly, or be told once.
Only one of those scales.

beats.authoring_note: fontSize 92 to clear the underfill floor. 'Ask' -> 'Subscribe' is the reel's actual misconception.

beats.narration_text: In a polling model, the client pulls — pinging the server over and over to see whether the task is finished. But A.I. models can take thirty seconds, or several minutes, to produce an answer. Poll that whole time and you will exhaust your rate limits long before the work completes. A webhook flips it into a push. You hand the server a U.R.L. and say: take your time, POST to this address when you are done.

beats.narration_text: So let's look at what a webhook actually is on the wire, because the answer is much less impressive than the word makes it sound.

beats.act: SCENE 3 — THE ANATOMY OF A WEBHOOK
beats.narration_text: A webhook is almost disappointingly simple. It is an automated HTTP POST, triggered by an event. A target U.R.L., a few headers, a JSON body. The sender does not care what you do with it — it fires the payload and forgets. That forgetting is exactly what keeps the two systems decoupled. It is also, as we are about to see, the problem.
beats.new_visual_element: The whole thing, on the wire

the signature header lands — the line that proves who sent it
the closing note lands: the sender fires and forgets

props.title: the whole protocol
props.code:
POST /hooks/done HTTP/1.1
Host: your-app.example
Content-Type: application/json
X-Signature: sha256=9f2c...   # who sent it

{
  "event": "job.completed",
  "id":    "evt_01HQ…",
  "result": { "total": 4500000 }
}

# That is the entire mechanism.
# The sender fires it and forgets.

beats.honesty_note: The signature header and the event id are shown deliberately: the script's Scene 3 mentions headers and auth in the visual but the VO does not explain them, and both become load-bearing in the falsifiability beat (signature proves the sender, id enables idempotent retries). The request shown is illustrative.

beats.narration_text: This is why webhooks are the backbone of modern automation. Pair them with an orchestrator like n8n or Zapier and one POST request triggers a cascade — alert the team in chat, email the client, update a database — all at once, all asynchronously, without your main application waiting for any of it.

beats.authoring_note: Uses connectors:false — the three destinations fire in PARALLEL, and connectors would assert a sequence the beat denies. Destinations are labelled generically (CHAT ALERT, CLIENT EMAIL) rather than using Slack or Gmail marks: a fidelity brand may not wear another product's chrome, and the point is the fan-out, not the vendor.

beats.narration_text: So where does this break? The sender forgets. That is the whole design — and it means nobody is tracking whether the message arrived. If your endpoint is down for thirty seconds, that event is simply gone, unless the sender retries. And if it does retry, you may now process the same event twice. Worse: an open webhook U.R.L. accepts a POST from anyone who finds it. Which is why the signature header is not decoration, and why every handler needs an event id it can recognise as a duplicate.

beats.authoring_note: BEAT ADDED — the script has no falsifiability scene (HOOK / PUSH VS PULL / ANATOMY / AUTOMATION / TASK). The ai-explainer arc requires one, and the genuine cost of fire-and-forget is that the decoupling which makes webhooks good is the same property that removes any delivery guarantee. Covers all three real consequences: silent loss, duplicate delivery on retry, and forged events against an open URL.

beats.narration_text: So stop burning compute on empty requests. Build systems that react to events instead of waiting for them — and write the handler as though the same event will arrive twice, because one day it will.

the idempotency note lands last — the line most handlers are missing

props.title: hook.py
props.code:
@app.post("/hooks/done")
def on_event(req):
    verify_signature(req)        # first, always
    if seen(req.json["id"]):     # idempotency
        return 200               # already handled
    handle(req.json)
    return 200

# TASK: stop polling. start pushing.

# Return 200 fast. Do the slow work
# after — senders time out and retry.

beats.authoring_note: The signature check, the idempotency guard and the return-200-fast note are the reel's additions. The script's task is a slogan; these are the three things that separate a webhook handler that works from one that looks like it works.

beats.narration_text: And here is the prompt worth running against your own handler. Ask a model what happens if the same event arrives three times, out of order, while your database is briefly unavailable. The answer tells you whether you built an event handler or just an endpoint that usually works.
